title: Iraq under the Ilkhans and the Turkmen
subtitle: 1258–1534 · A Ruined Province Ruled from Tabriz — the Mongol Peace, the Jalayirid Flicker, Timur's Skulls, the Black and White Sheep, and the Ottoman–Safavid Frontier Fixed on Iraq

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Ilkhanid Iraq governed from Tabriz, the Jalayirids making Baghdad a capital again, Timur's two sacks, the Kara Koyunlu and Ak Koyunlu Turkmen confederations, the Safavid conquest and the forced Shia turn, the Ottoman conquest, and the tribes who were the real power

entries.label: Ilkhanid Iraq, governed from Tabriz
entries.hint: For eighty years Iraq was a province of the Ilkhanate, ruled by a viceroy from Tabriz or Sultaniyya far to the north. Ghazan's conversion to Islam in 1295 and his vizier Rashid al-Din's reforms brought a partial recovery; his brother Öljeitü briefly made Twelver Shi'ism the state creed. When the last Ilkhan, Abu Sa'id, died without an heir in 1335, the state came apart and Iraq was up for grabs.
entries.note: Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'; Charles Melville, 'The Fall of Amir Chupan and the Decline of the Ilkhanate' (1999).

entries.label: The Jalayirids make Baghdad a capital again
entries.hint: A Mongol-descended house, the Jalayirids picked Iraq out of the wreck of the Ilkhanate and, under Shaykh Uways and then the poet-king Sultan Ahmad, gave Baghdad a last spell as a court city — with painters, poets and building. It did not last: Sultan Ahmad fled Timur twice, was sheltered by the Mamluks, came back, and was killed by the Turkmen in 1410; the dynasty's last remnant was swept up by 1432.
entries.note: Patrick Wing, 'The Jalayirids: Dynastic State Formation in the Mongol Middle East' (2016).

entries.label: Timur and the two sacks of Baghdad
entries.hint: Timur took Baghdad in 1393 and lost it when he moved on; he came back in 1401, stormed it after a siege pressed home on a fast-day, and this time ordered a general massacre — every soldier to bring back at least two severed heads. The chronicles count a hundred and twenty towers built of the skulls. He then withdrew, leaving Iraq to the Turkmen and a ruin deeper than the Mongols had made.
entries.note: Ibn ʿArabshah, 'ʿAjāʾib al-Maqdūr'; Sharaf al-Din ʿAli Yazdi, 'Ẓafarnāma'; Beatrice Manz, 'The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane' (1989).

entries.label: The Black Sheep Turkmen
entries.hint: Qara Yusuf's confederation of the Black Sheep Turkmen ruled Iraq and Azerbaijan from Tabriz, holding Baghdad through a governing prince. Under Jahan Shah, who briefly took most of Iran, it was a great power. But it was a tribal confederation, not a state — its Baghdad prince, Pir Budaq, rebelled and had to be besieged and killed — and Jahan Shah's death in battle in 1467 ended it.
entries.note: John Woods, 'The Aqquyunlu: Clan, Confederation, Empire' (1999); Faruk Sümer, 'Kara Koyunlular' (1967).

entries.label: The White Sheep Turkmen
entries.hint: Uzun Hasan of the White Sheep Turkmen destroyed the Kara Koyunlu in 1467 and built a state from Diyarbakir to central Iran, with Baghdad a frontier governorship. He looked west for allies — his envoys reached Venice — but his tribal cavalry was smashed by Ottoman guns at Otlukbeli in 1473, and after his son Ya'qub the dynasty tore itself apart, leaving the field to a new force out of Ardabil.
entries.note: John Woods, 'The Aqquyunlu' (1999).

entries.label: The Safavid conquest and the Shia turn
entries.hint: Shah Isma'il took Baghdad in 1508 and made Twelver Shi'ism the law. He and his officers rebuilt and gilded the shrines of Najaf, Karbala and Kazimayn and dug a canal to bring water to Najaf — and, in the same years, wrecked the tomb of Abu Hanifa and the shrine of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, the great Sunni sites, and killed Sunnis in numbers. Iraq had become the front line of a religious war.
entries.note: the Safavid chronicles in Roger Savory, 'Iran under the Safavids' (1980); Rasul Jaʿfariyan on the shrine cities.

entries.label: Suleiman takes Baghdad
entries.hint: In the winter of 1534 Sultan Suleiman marched on Baghdad; the Safavid governor abandoned it, and the sultan entered without a fight at the end of November. He prayed at the Sunni shrines and restored them, visited the Shia ones, and organised Iraq as an Ottoman province. The city changed hands again in the next century, but the frontier settled near where it runs today, and Iraq was tied to the Ottoman world for four hundred years.
entries.note: Feridun Emecen, 'Osmanlı İmparatorluğu'nun Kuruluş ve Yükseliş Tarihi' (2015); Rhoads Murphey, 'Ottoman Warfare 1500–1700' (1999).

entries.label: The tribes, the Kurds and the Musha'sha'
entries.hint: Under every distant dynasty the country outside the towns belonged to its own powers: the great Bedouin confederations of the desert and the Jazira, the Marsh Arabs of the south, the hereditary Kurdish emirs of the northern mountains, and — from the 1430s — the Musha'sha', a militant Shia movement that grew out of the Hilla schools, gathered the marsh tribes, and held Wasit, Hilla and Basra at various times. These were the real governments most people knew.
entries.note: 'Abbas al-'Azzawi, 'Ta'rīkh al-'Irāq bayn Iḥtilālayn' (1935–56); Pierre-Jean Luizard on the Mushaʿshaʿ.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Ilkhanate's dissolution and the war of the amirs, Timur's campaigns and the tower of skulls, the Turkmen displacing the Jalayirids, Otlukbeli and the lesson of firearms, the Safavid conquest and the sectarian massacres, and Suleiman's bloodless entry into Baghdad

entries.group: The End of the Mongol Peace
entries.label: The dissolution of the Ilkhanate
entries.hint: When Abu Sa'id died in 1335 leaving no son, the Ilkhanate broke into the private wars of its great amirs — the Chupanids in the north, the Jalayirids around Baghdad, a run of puppet khans between them. Iraq was fought back and forth for a generation before the Jalayirids came out on top. Unified rule over the whole Mongol Middle East was finished, and Iraq slid back to being a piece of a smaller pie.
entries.note: Charles Melville, 'The Fall of Amir Chupan' (1999); Patrick Wing, 'The Jalayirids' (2016).

entries.label: Timur's campaigns and the tower of skulls
entries.hint: Timur passed through Iraq twice with fire and sword — reducing the fortress of Tikrit and raising a tower of skulls there in 1393, then in 1401 taking Baghdad by storm and ordering the massacre that built a hundred and twenty more. He also broke the Kurdish and Bedouin lords and the towns of the Jazira. The country he left behind was more thoroughly wrecked than at any point since the Mongol invasion.
entries.note: Ibn ʿArabshah, 'ʿAjāʾib al-Maqdūr'; Yazdi, 'Ẓafarnāma'.

entries.label: The Turkmen displace the Jalayirids
entries.hint: Qara Yusuf of the Black Sheep and Sultan Ahmad Jalayir allied against Timur's heirs, retook their lands — and then turned on each other. Qara Yusuf defeated and killed Ahmad near Tabriz in 1410 and took Baghdad in 1411; the last Jalayirid holdouts in Basra and Hilla were mopped up by 1432. The Turkmen tribal confederations now held Iraq, and would for a century.
entries.note: John Woods, 'The Aqquyunlu' (1999); Patrick Wing, 'The Jalayirids' (2016).

entries.label: Otlukbeli and the lesson of firearms
entries.hint: Uzun Hasan of the White Sheep wiped out the Black Sheep in 1467, inherited Iraq, and then marched against the Ottomans. At Otlukbeli in 1473 his tribal horse-archers met an Ottoman army with massed muskets and field artillery and were destroyed. The Turkmen had conquered with cavalry and had not adopted the new weapons; the battle showed that the age of the pure tribal army was ending.
entries.note: John Woods, 'The Aqquyunlu' (1999); Rhoads Murphey, 'Ottoman Warfare' (1999).

entries.label: The Safavid conquest and the sectarian war
entries.hint: Isma'il's Qizilbash cavalry broke the last Ak Koyunlu at Sharur in 1501, took Tabriz, and by 1508 held Baghdad. The conquest came with a programme: Twelver Shi'ism enforced, Sunni scholars killed or driven out, and the tombs of Abu Hanifa and al-Jilani desecrated. The Ottomans answered in kind against Shia in their lands. The confessional war that would define Iraq's next four centuries had begun.
entries.note: Roger Savory, 'Iran under the Safavids' (1980); Andrew Newman, 'Safavid Iran' (2006).

entries.label: The fall of Baghdad to Suleiman
entries.hint: In the first Ottoman–Safavid war Suleiman led the Two Iraqs campaign south through Azerbaijan and into the Sawad. The Safavid governor of Baghdad fled rather than fight, and the sultan entered the city without resistance at the end of 1534. The peace that followed set the Ottoman–Safavid line close to the modern Iraq–Iran border and made Iraq an Ottoman frontier province against Shia Iran.
entries.note: Rhoads Murphey, 'Ottoman Warfare 1500–1700' (1999); Feridun Emecen (2015).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A province ruled from elsewhere, the Ilkhanid fiscal reforms and their limits, the endowed shrine administrations that every regime patronised, the tribal order at its widest, the Turkmen confederation as a form of state, and the coming Sunni–Shia frontier

entries.label: A province of a state centred to the north
entries.hint: Through almost the whole period Iraq — 'Arab Iraq', as against the Persian Iraq of the Iranian plateau — was a peripheral province of a power seated at Tabriz, Sultaniyya, Herat, Diyarbakir or, at the end, Istanbul. It got a governor, a garrison and a tax demand, and little else. The habit of being administered from outside the country began here and lasted, in one form or another, into the twentieth century.
entries.note: 'Abbas al-'Azzawi, 'Ta'rīkh al-'Irāq bayn Iḥtilālayn' (1935–56); Michael Morony on the longue durée.

entries.label: The Ilkhanid reforms and their limits
entries.hint: Ghazan and his vizier Rashid al-Din tried to reverse the ruin: fixed tax rates in place of the arbitrary levy, a reformed silver coinage, a survey of the land, incentives to bring waste ground back under the plough, protection for the peasant against the passing soldier. The edicts survive in Rashid al-Din's collected papers. The effort was real, and it did not outlast the dynasty's collapse in 1335.
entries.note: Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh' and the 'Mukātabāt-i Rashīdī'; I. P. Petrushevsky, 'The Socio-Economic Condition of Iran under the Il-Khans' (1968).

entries.label: The shrine administrations
entries.hint: The one set of institutions that survived every sack were the shrine complexes — the Shia sanctuaries at Najaf, Karbala, Kazimayn and Samarra, and the Sunni tombs of Abu Hanifa and Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani in Baghdad. Each was an endowed foundation with its own revenues, staff, and (at the Shia shrines) a growing resident body of scholars and students. Every regime, Sunni or Shia, felt bound to patronise them, which is much of why they endured.
entries.note: Meir Litvak, 'Shiʿi Scholars of Nineteenth-Century Iraq' (1998), on the background; Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994).

entries.label: The tribal order at its widest
entries.hint: With the farmland gone, most of Iraq was governed by tribal shaykhs: the Bedouin confederations of the desert who taxed or raided the caravans, the Marsh Arabs of the south, the hereditary Kurdish emirs of the mountains. They paid a token tribute to whoever claimed the country, supplied cavalry when it suited, and were left alone otherwise. The pastoral-nomadic share of the population was at its historical peak.
entries.note: 'Abbas al-'Azzawi (1935–56); Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981), on the settlement collapse.

entries.label: The Turkmen confederation as a form of state
entries.hint: The Black Sheep and the White Sheep were not states but confederations: the ruler was first among the tribal chiefs, the army was their cavalry, the princes held apanages, and every succession was a war. It was a form that could conquer a great deal of territory very fast and could not administer it, keep a treasury, or field the new gunpowder infantry. The bureaucratic empires on either side eventually ate it.
entries.note: John Woods, 'The Aqquyunlu: Clan, Confederation, Empire' (1999).

entries.label: The Sunni–Shia state frontier
entries.hint: Öljeitü's brief Shia state in 1310 was a foretaste; the Safavid seizure of Iran in 1501 made it structural. From then on Iraq was the ground where the confessional border of Islam — Shia Iran against the Sunni Ottomans — was fought over and, by the mid-seventeenth century, fixed. The shrine cities ended up on the Shia side of the line and the government on the Sunni side, a tension built into the country.
entries.note: Colin Imber, 'The Ottoman Empire, 1300–1650' (2002); Andrew Newman, 'Safavid Iran' (2006).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The shrine cities and the Shia clerical presence at Hilla then Najaf, Ghazan's conversion and Öljeitü's Shia experiment, the Sufi orders as the popular religion, the Safavid order that became a state, the reduced Jews and Christians, and the millenarians of the marshes

entries.label: Hilla, Najaf, and the making of the atabat
entries.hint: In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the leading centre of Twelver learning was Hilla, on the Euphrates, home of the jurists al-Muhaqqiq and al-Allama al-Hilli. Over the following centuries the seminary weight shifted south to Najaf, beside the tomb of Ali, and Najaf, Karbala, Kazimayn and Samarra together became the atabat, the 'thresholds' — a Shia holy land of pilgrimage, study and burial that gave Iraq a role nothing else could.
entries.note: Yitzhak Nakash, 'The Shiʿis of Iraq' (1994); Andrew Newman, 'The Formative Period of Twelver Shīʿism' (2000).

entries.label: Ghazan's conversion and Öljeitü's Shia experiment
entries.hint: In 1295 the Ilkhan Ghazan and much of the Mongol elite converted to Islam — a turning point for the whole region, and the end of the Buddhist and shamanist presence in Iran and Iraq. His brother Öljeitü went further: persuaded by the jurist al-Hilli, he adopted Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion in 1310, striking coins in the names of the Twelve Imams. It did not survive him, but it showed what was possible.
entries.note: Judith Pfeiffer, 'Conversion Versions: Sultan Öljeytü's Conversion to Shiʿism' (1999); Charles Melville on Ghazan.

entries.label: The Sufi orders as the common faith
entries.hint: For most people religion meant an order and a shrine. The Qadiriyya centred on al-Jilani's tomb in Baghdad, which grew a quarter of its own; the Rifa'iyya spread from the southern marshes with its ecstatic rites; the Turkmen carried the Bektashiyya and kindred orders; the Kubrawiyya worked the north. The lodge, the saint's grave and the annual festival were the framework of ordinary devotion under every dynasty.
entries.note: J. Spencer Trimingham, 'The Sufi Orders in Islam' (1971); Thomas Emil Homerin on the Rifāʿiyya.

entries.label: The Safaviyya
entries.hint: The Safaviyya began as a respectable Sunni Sufi order at Ardabil. Over the fifteenth century its leaders militarised it, gathered a following among the Turkmen tribes — the Qizilbash, the 'red-heads' — and turned its teaching into a messianic Shia creed that made the shaykh a near-divine figure. In 1501 the boy Isma'il led it to a throne. A Sufi brotherhood had become an empire, and it imposed Twelver Shi'ism wherever it reached.
entries.note: Kathryn Babayan, 'Mystics, Monarchs, and Messiahs' (2002); Roger Savory, 'Iran under the Safavids' (1980).

entries.label: The Jews and Christians of Iraq, reduced
entries.hint: The old communities were much diminished. Baghdad's Jews were now a small body led by a nasi rather than an exilarch, though the tomb of Ezekiel at Kifl stayed a great pilgrimage site and drew patronage. The Church of the East, gutted by Timur's massacres, pulled its patriarch back from Baghdad into the Kurdish mountains and shrank to a highland-and-Malabar core; the split that produced the Chaldean Church lay just ahead.
entries.note: Zvi Yehuda, 'The New Babylonian Diaspora' (2017); David Wilmshurst, 'The Martyred Church' (2011).

entries.label: The millenarians of the Musha'sha'
entries.hint: Muhammad ibn Falah, trained in the Hilla schools, declared himself the gate to the Hidden Imam — and then, to his teachers' horror, something more — gathered the Arab tribes of the lower Euphrates and Khuzestan marshes, and founded a militant Shia state around 1436 that seized Wasit, Hilla and Basra at different times. The marsh had sheltered heterodox movements since antiquity; it did so again.
entries.note: Pierre-Jean Luizard, 'La formation de l'Irak contemporain' (1991), on the Mushaʿshaʿ; the entry in EI2.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Rashid al-Din and the first world history, the Jalayirid school of painting, Persian and Turkic poetry at the Turkmen courts and Fuzuli of Baghdad, the Mirjan complex and the shrine building, and Arabic learning holding in the shrine cities

entries.label: Rashid al-Din and the first world history
entries.hint: The Ilkhanid vizier Rashid al-Din, a physician and a converted Jew, assembled with a team at his scholarly suburb of Tabriz the Compendium of Chronicles — a history not just of the Mongols and the Muslims but of the Chinese, the Indians, the Franks and the Jews, gathered from informants of each. It is the first genuine world history, and a monument of the moment when Iraq was a corner of a Eurasian empire. Rashid al-Din was executed in 1318 and his complex looted.
entries.note: Rashid al-Din, 'Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh'; Stefan Kamola, 'Making Mongol History: Rashid al-Din and the Jamiʿ al-Tawarikh' (2019).

entries.label: The Jalayirid school of painting
entries.hint: Under Sultan Uways and Sultan Ahmad, Baghdad and Tabriz produced a brief, exquisite flowering of the illustrated book — the Diwan of Sultan Ahmad, a great Kalila wa-Dimna, Shahnama and Khamsa manuscripts, the painter Junayd — with a new delicacy of line, landscape and colour. The workshops scattered when Timur came, and their style went east and became the foundation of Timurid painting at Herat.
entries.note: Deborah Klimburg-Salter, 'A Sufi Theme in Persian Painting: The Diwan of Sultan Ahmad Ǧalāʾir' (1976); Sheila Blair & Jonathan Bloom, 'The Art and Architecture of Islam 1250–1800' (1994).

entries.label: Poetry at the Turkmen courts, and Fuzuli
entries.hint: Persian poetry held the Jalayirid and Turkmen courts — Khwaju Kirmani worked at Baghdad, Jahan Shah of the Black Sheep wrote a divan — and Turkic verse rose beside it, in the poems of the young Shah Isma'il. The age's giant was Fuzuli, a man of a Turkmen family who spent his life among the shrine cities and wrote, in Turkish, Persian and Arabic, lyric poetry — above all the Leyla and Mejnun — that has never been surpassed in the Turkish language.
entries.note: the 'Dīvān' and 'Leylā vü Mecnūn' of Fuzuli; the study by Hamide Demirel, 'The Poet Fuzûlî' (1991).

entries.label: The Mirjan complex and the shrine building
entries.hint: Little was built, and little of that survives, but the Jalayirid governor Amin al-Din Mirjan left Baghdad a madrasa and a great caravanserai, the Khan Mirjan, whose hall is roofed by a remarkable set of intersecting transverse brick vaults — a technical high point. Most of the period's real investment went into the shrines: the domes and courts of Najaf, Karbala and Kazimayn were extended and, under the Safavids, gilded.
entries.note: K. A. C. Creswell & James Allan, 'A Short Account of Early Muslim Architecture' (1989); the Khan Mirjan in the Iraqi antiquities surveys.

entries.label: Arabic learning holds in the shrine cities
entries.hint: With Baghdad wrecked, Arabic-Islamic scholarship in Iraq retreated to the peripheries and specialised: Hilla and then Najaf for Twelver law and hadith, the surviving Baghdad madrasas and the Kurdish ulama for the Sunni tradition, Basra for grammar and transmission. The great biographical and reference works of the age were now written in Cairo and Damascus, drawing on chains of transmission that still ran through Iraq but no longer originated there.
entries.note: 'Abbas al-'Azzawi, 'Ta'rīkh al-'Irāq' (1935–56); Devin Stewart on the Ḥilla school.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Maragha observatory and the last great moment of Islamic astronomy, al-Hilli and the systematising of Twelver law and ijtihad, the age of compilation and commentary, and the Sufi metaphysics of the unity of being

entries.label: The Maragha observatory
entries.hint: The year after the sack of Baghdad, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi talked Hulagu into funding an observatory at Maragha, just north in Azerbaijan, with a great library — partly the salvage of the ruined city — and an international staff that included a Chinese astronomer. Out of it came the Ilkhanid Tables and a set of new planetary models, the 'Tusi couple' among them, that turn up three centuries later in the work of Copernicus.
entries.note: George Saliba, 'Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance' (2007); F. Jamil Ragep, 'Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī's Memoir on Astronomy' (1993).

entries.label: al-Hilli and the systematising of Twelver law
entries.hint: At Hilla, al-Muhaqqiq al-Hilli and his nephew al-Allama al-Hilli wrote the works that fixed the shape of Twelver jurisprudence, formally established independent legal reasoning, ijtihad, as its method, and set up the ranking of qualified jurists. The autonomous clerical institution that would make Najaf a power in its own right centuries later was given its intellectual scaffolding here.
entries.note: al-Allama al-Hilli, 'Mabādiʾ al-Wuṣūl' and 'Tadhkirat al-Fuqahāʾ'; Devin Stewart, 'Islamic Legal Orthodoxy' (1998).

entries.label: Commentary, recension and the reference work
entries.hint: Original work was scarce and the age's energy went into consolidation: al-Tusi's clean recensions of Euclid, Ptolemy and the 'middle books' that became the standard teaching texts across the Islamic world; the biographical dictionary of Baghdad by Ibn al-Fuwati; the multiplying commentaries and glosses of the madrasa. It was a conservationist phase — passing the inheritance on rather than adding to it.
entries.note: A. I. Sabra on the recension tradition; Ibn al-Fuwati, 'Majmaʿ al-Ādāb fī Muʿjam al-Alqāb'.

entries.label: The Sufi metaphysics of the unity of being
entries.hint: The school of Ibn Arabi — the doctrine that all existence is one, a single divine reality showing itself in many forms — spread through the Sufi orders and became the dominant intellectual and poetic mode of the whole post-Mongol Persianate world. In Iraq it was carried by the Qadiri and Kubrawi lodges and voiced in the verse of Fakhr al-Din Iraqi and, later, echoes of Jami. Metaphysics had moved from the madrasa to the lodge.
entries.note: William Chittick, 'The Sufi Path of Knowledge' (1989); the 'Lamaʿāt' of Fakhr al-Din ʿIraqi.
